content: In 2012, the World Health Organization (WHO) initiated the development of a guideline focused on optimal serum and red blood cell folate concentrations in women of reproductive age to prevent neural tube defects (NTDs). This effort involved representatives from all WHO departments and was overseen by a steering committee that provided guidance and supervision throughout the process. Two additional groups were formed: an advisory guideline group and an external review group. The guideline development group was specifically established for this project, and its participants are listed in Annex 3. Their role was to advise WHO on selecting critical outcomes for decision-making and interpreting the evidence. The WHO guideline development group included experts from various WHO expert advisory panels and specialists identified through open calls. The selection process ensured a balanced gender representation, multidisciplinary expertise, and regional representation from all WHO regions. Efforts were made to include content experts, methodologists, stakeholders (such as health professionals involved in nutrition surveillance), and technical staff from WHO and health ministries of Member States. Representatives of commercial organizations were excluded from membership in the guideline group. External reviewers were identified through WHO Nutrition mailing lists and the WHO Nutrition website, which collectively reach over 5,500 subscribers. A public call for comments ensured proper interpretation of the recommendations. Additionally, three content experts peer-reviewed the draft guideline and provided technical input, as detailed in Annex 4. The scope of the guideline and evidence appraisal began with drafting key questions by technical staff from the Evidence and Programme Guidance Unit, Department of Nutrition for Health and Development. These questions addressed the relationship between blood folate levels, folate intake, and NTD risk, drawing on in vitro, animal, and human studies. The methodological approach for retrieving, summarizing, and assessing evidence quality was discussed with relevant stakeholders. A formal guideline development group meeting was held in Geneva, Switzerland, from September 23–25, 2013. Systematic reviews and GRADE evidence profiles were used to draft the guideline, and the draft recommendations were discussed by the WHO steering committee and the guideline development group during the meeting. Decision-making procedures were established at the start of the meeting, including rules for agreement and consensus. The guideline development group deliberated on the wording of the recommendations and reached consensus without major disagreements. Factors considered included the quality of evidence, values and preferences related to the intervention, its desirable and undesirable effects, and the cost of available options in different settings. Consensus was defined as agreement by a simple majority with no dissent. Cost, feasibility, and values were also considered, and implementation considerations were widely discussed and documented. WHO staff and external technical experts involved in evidence collection and grading were not allowed to participate in decision-making. The majority of the group agreed that the recommendation was strong or conditional. Three content experts peer-reviewed the draft guideline, and a public call for comments was issued on January 16, 2015. Seventeen external reviewers registered, providing declarations of interest and their CVs. Ten external reviewers reviewed the draft guideline, as detailed in Annex 5. WHO staff finalized the guideline and submitted it for clearance before publication. Management of competing interests followed WHO's rules, requiring all experts to declare relevant interests before participation. Declarations of interest were reviewed by the responsible technical officer and relevant departments before finalizing the group composition. Participants submitted declarations of interest and CVs before each meeting and verbally declared potential conflicts of interest at the start of each meeting. Procedures for managing conflicts of interest adhered to WHO guidelines. Experts participated in their individual capacity, not as institutional representatives. Dr. Lynn Bailey, a professor at the University of Georgia, declared interests related to folate status and its impact on maternal and child health, as well as the interaction of folate with other nutrients. She also declared authorship of manuscripts and books on folate nutrition and membership in the BOND Folate Group. Her interests were documented, and she participated fully. Dr. Anne Molloy, a researcher at Trinity College Dublin, focuses on the metabolic functions of folate and vitamin B12, particularly genetic polymorphisms as risk factors for NTDs. She declared co-authorship of a key reference used in the guideline and recused herself from consensus decision-making regarding its selection as the main data source. Dr. Christine Pfeiffer, Chief of the Nutritional Biomarkers Branch at the CDC, specializes in analytical methods for nutritional biomarkers and their application in epidemiologic studies. She has authored over 100 peer-reviewed manuscripts and contributed to major agency reports on nutritional biomarkers. Her interests were documented, and she participated fully. Other guideline development group members, all experts in folic acid and congenital anomalies, declared their intellectual interests, which did not preclude their full participation in decision-making. Dr. Irma Silva-Zolezzi, employed by Nestlé Research Center, declared a previous grant from Nestlé and presented on the global distribution of the MTHFR 677C→T polymorphism. She was notified that, as an external expert, she would not participate in decision-making. The guideline is scheduled for review in 2024. The WHO Department of Nutrition for Health and Development in Geneva will coordinate the update, following formal WHO procedures. WHO welcomes suggestions for additional questions to evaluate during the review.
